Abstract
Optimizing the scheduling of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) is a critical task in the context of smart manufacturing, 
particularly in Industry 4.0, where operational efficiency, sustainability, and adaptability are key drivers of innovation. 
This paper introduces an innovative scheduling model incorporating real-time AGV battery status as a key parameter, 
using a machine learning algorithm to predict energy consumption and optimize task allocation accordingly. The primary 
objective is to extend AGV battery life, reduce energy consumption, and contribute to environmental sustainability, all 
while maintaining high operational efficiency. In addition to the scheduling algorithm, we present a comprehensive appli­
cation framework designed to integrate this optimization model into real-world factory environments. This architecture 
leverages cloud-edge computing to process real-time data from AGVs, enabling dynamic scheduling adjustments and 
seamless execution of tasks. The proposed approach has been experimentally validated, demonstrating improvements in 
energy efficiency when compared to a conventional AGV scheduling strategy. This result demonstrates the effectiveness 
of our solution in improving energy efficiency while maintaining high performance in AGV operations. By providing the 
necessary infrastructure for data input, processing, and output implementation, the framework ensures that the algorithm 
can be effectively deployed and scaled in industrial settings. This research offers a robust solution for AGV scheduling, 
balancing operational efficiency with sustainability.

A critical component in this smart manufacturing eco­

(AGVs). These autonomous, sensor-equipped vehicles are 
designed to transport materials within manufacturing facili­
ties with minimal human intervention (Bechtsis et al. 2017). 
Over the past few decades, AGVs have evolved from sim­
ple, pre-programmed robots to sophisticated systems capa­
ble of navigating complex environments using advanced 
sensors, navigation algorithms, and decision-making sys­
tems. In modern factories, AGVs have become indispens­
able for material handling tasks, including the transport of 
raw materials to production lines, the movement of semi-
finished products between processes, and the delivery of 
finished goods to storage or shipping areas. Their ability to 
operate continuously, avoid obstacles, and adapt to chang­
ing operational conditions makes them a critical asset in 
achieving the efficiency, flexibility, and scalability required 
by Industry 4.0.
Despite their advantages, the effective deployment of 
AGVs in smart manufacturing environments presents a set 
of significant challenges, particularly concerning real-time 
scheduling and routing (Fragapane et al. 2021). Given the 
dynamic nature of production environments, where orders, 
production priorities, and material availability can change 
rapidly, scheduling must be highly adaptive. Traditional 
static scheduling approaches are inadequate in such sce­
narios, as they are not capable of responding effectively 
to fluctuations in demand or unforeseen disruptions, such 
as equipment breakdowns or sudden changes in produc­
tion schedules. Furthermore, as the number of AGVs in 
a facility increases, so does the complexity of coordinat­
ing their movements to avoid collisions, bottlenecks, and 
under-utilization.
A critical constraint in AGV operations is battery life. 
Since AGVs rely on rechargeable batteries, their opera­
tional efficiency is significantly impacted by the state of 
battery charge, necessitating frequent recharging events. 
Such frequent recharging not only introduces consider­
able downtime but also accelerates battery degradation, 
increasing operational costs and environmental impact 
related to battery disposal (Theunissen et al. 2018; Zhang 
et al. 2023). Furthermore, the necessity to route AGVs peri­
odically to charging stations poses logistical challenges, 
potentially causing interruptions in ongoing material han­
dling processes. Therefore, efficiently balancing continu­
ous operation and battery capacity constraints represents a 
fundamental issue in modern AGV scheduling approaches 
(Dang et al. 2021).
To address these challenges, this research proposes a 
novel machine learning-based algorithm for AGV schedul­
ing that considers real-time battery status and energy con­
sumption patterns. Unlike traditional scheduling approaches, 
which often rely on fixed parameters and assumptions, our 
approach leverages historical and real-time data to predict 
when an AGV will require recharging and dynamically 
adjusts its task schedule accordingly. By using machine 
learning techniques to predict energy consumption, the 
algorithm optimizes AGV utilization, ensuring that vehicles 
are assigned to the most critical tasks while efficiently rout­
ing them to charging stations, minimizing downtime and 
maximizing throughput.
In contrast, traditional mathematical models in the lit­
erature often make simplifying assumptions that limit their 
applicability in dynamic, real-world environments. For 
example, many AGV scheduling models assume constant 
energy consumption rates regardless of load or travel path. 
As highlighted by Boccia et al. (2023) in their study, many 
models overlook the impact of varying energy consumption 
due to factors such as the weight of transported materials 
and the length of the routes. This assumption leads to inac­
curacies when applied in real-world scenarios where such 
variables significantly affect battery performance.
Similarly, Xiao et al. (2024) propose a model that inte­
grates battery swapping and speed control into AGV sched­
uling. Their approach acknowledges that charging times are 
not constant and vary based on the battery’s state of charge. 
This model addresses the complexities of AGV fleet opera­
tions in automated container terminals, considering factors 
such as energy consumption, operational delays, and the 
need for efficient coordination to minimize disruptions in 
material handling processes.
These assumptions, while useful for theoretical explo­
ration, significantly limit the practicality of such models 
in environments that require real-time decision-making 
and adaptability. In contrast, our machine learning-based 
approach removes the need for such fixed assumptions by 
continuously learning from operational data. This allows 
the system to adapt dynamically to the complexities and 
uncertainties of real-world AGV operations, improving

2  Related works
2.1  Towards cloud-to-edge computing in intelligent 
manufacturing
The cloud-to-edge computing paradigm is transforming 
intelligent manufacturing, enabling real-time, distributed 
processing while maintaining the computational power and 
storage capabilities of cloud systems. This hybrid approach 
has emerged as a response to the limitations of centralized 
cloud infrastructures, especially in latency-sensitive envi­
ronments where immediate decision-making is crucial. This 
section reviews state-of-the-art research on cloud-to-edge 
architectures relevant to Industry 4.0, highlighting the inte­
gration of various technologies to enhance manufacturing 
processes (Chiappa et al. 2023).
One of the foundational elements in modern smart manu­
facturing is the hybrid architecture that combines cloud 
and edge computing. Edge computing reduces the load on 
centralized cloud servers by processing data closer to the 
source, enabling low-latency responses and real-time ana­
lytics. In this context, Chekired et al. (2018) proposed a fog 
computing model where data is processed in multiple layers 
edge, fog, and cloud based on the computational intensity 
of the task. This model has been applied in Industrial IoT 
(IIoT) environments to optimize data scheduling and real-
time decision-making on the shop floor. Similarly, Wang 
et al. (2020) introduced a micro-service-based architecture 
that integrates cloud and edge resources for smart manufac­
turing. Their work demonstrated how micro-services allow 
dynamic task allocation between cloud and edge layers, 
ensuring that latency-sensitive tasks, such as real-time qual­
ity control, are handled at the edge while more resource-
intensive computations are offloaded to the cloud.
In addition to the hybrid models, edge computing has 
proven instrumental in applications such as predictive 
maintenance, fault diagnosis, and process optimization.

2.2  Advances in AGV scheduling: optimization 
methods and energy-aware solutions
The scheduling of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) is 
a well-studied problem within the broader context of smart 
manufacturing. Several methodologies and approaches have 
been developed to optimize the scheduling and routing of 
AGVs, addressing key operational challenges such as mini­
mizing travel time, avoiding collisions, and managing bat­
tery life. In this section, we review the literature on AGV 
scheduling, highlighting mathematical models, heuristic 
approaches, and optimization techniques commonly used in 
the field.
Scheduling Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) is criti­
cal for operational efficiency in Flexible Manufacturing 
Systems (FMS). Recent studies have categorized AGV-
related research into key areas such as flow-path design, 
dispatching, and vehicle routing. These studies emphasize 
the importance of optimizing flow-path layouts and vehicle 
dispatching strategies to reduce travel times and enhance 
overall system productivity (Bathla et al. 2022). Building 
on this foundation, Qiu et al. (2015) focused on scheduling 
and routing algorithms for AGVs, presenting an in-depth 
survey of the key strategies used to optimize both sched­
uling and routing. These works identified the Dial-a-Ride 
Problem (DARP) as a central challenge in AGV schedul­
ing, where vehicles must be optimally routed to minimize 
total travel time while adhering to operational constraints 
such as battery life and load capacity. Other works explored 
the integration of routing problems within the AGV con­
text, expanding the classic Dial-a-Ride Problem (DARP) to 
accommodate the specifics of electric autonomous vehicles 
(e-ADARP) (Bongiovanni et al. 2019). Integrating battery 
management detours to charging stations and other related 
operational constraints aims to optimize travel and ride time 
through a sophisticated mixed-integer linear programming 
approach and a branch-and-cut algorithm.
Tang et al. (2019) developed a reconfigurable cloud-edge 
framework that facilitates flexible and scalable intelligent 
manufacturing. Their architecture allows manufacturers to 
dynamically adapt to changes in production requirements 
by redistributing computational loads between the edge and 
cloud.
Another notable application of edge computing is seen 
in the deployment of digital twins. Digital twins are virtual 
models of physical assets that rely on real-time data from 
edge devices to continuously adjust operational parameters. 
The Pan et al. (2021) study on digital twin-driven production 
logistics demonstrated the effectiveness of edge computing 
in ensuring real-time synchronization between physical and 
digital environments.
Fog computing, often considered an extension of edge 
computing, plays a crucial role in handling intermedi­
ary processing tasks, particularly in smart factories. By 
deploying computational nodes closer to the operational 
edge, fog computing ensures that time-critical data is pro­
cessed locally, reducing latency and bandwidth usage. This 
approach enables real-time decision-making and automa­
tion, essential for optimizing operations in industrial envi­
ronments (Zhou et al. 2023).
In the same vein, Muniswamaiah et al. (2021) emphasize 
the role of fog computing in the Internet of Things (IoT), 
outlining its potential to bridge the gap between cloud infra­
structure and edge devices by handling both data storage 
and processing at intermediate layers. Their model has been 
instrumental in improving operational efficiency, reducing 
cloud dependency, and enabling real-time analytics in criti­
cal industrial applications.
With the growing complexity of manufacturing pro­
cesses, AI-driven edge computing is gaining traction. Cao 
et al. (2020) developed a framework for integrating machine 
learning models into edge devices, allowing real-time fault 
detection and predictive analytics without relying on the 
cloud. This approach not only reduces latency but also 
increases the autonomy of manufacturing systems, enabling 
quicker responses to unexpected events. Moreover, Zhang 
et al. proposed a multi-agent-based collaborative manufac­
turing environment that uses edge computing to distribute 
AI tasks across a network of devices. This architecture sup­
ports collaborative decision-making between autonomous 
systems, enhancing the scalability and flexibility of the 
manufacturing process.
While cloud-to-edge computing offers numerous 
advantages, several challenges remain (Nain et al. 2022). 
Interoperability between legacy systems and modern edge-
computing frameworks continues to pose difficulties, espe­
cially in manufacturing environments where older machines 
may not easily integrate with new technologies. Furthermore, 
the security of data processed at the edge requires robust

Recent studies have reviewed various methods for opti­
mizing AGV routing and scheduling, including exact, heu­
ristic, and metaheuristic approaches. These studies highlight 
the importance of combining multiple strategies to address 
complex industrial applications where real-time responsive­
ness is critical (Bhargava et al. 2024). Furthermore, Kaoud

job shop, flow shop, and container terminal applications, 
proposing potential future research directions for improv­
ing scheduling efficiency. These studies emphasized the

More recent research has focused on multi-objective 
scheduling, where AGV systems must balance multiple con­

decentralized control strategies for AGVs, focusing on task

proposed innovative methods for managing AGV fleets in 
highly dynamic environments, emphasizing the importance 
of distributed control systems. Similar research extends the 
classical multiple Traveling Salesman Problem (mTSP), 
incorporating drone stations to facilitate quicker delivery 
solutions (Kloster et al. 2023) and significantly reduce the 
makespan. The study employs a mixed integer linear pro­
gramming (MILP) model and a mathematical approach to 
tackle more significant instances effectively.
Battery life is a critical constraint in AGV scheduling, 
particularly in large-scale manufacturing operations. Singh 
et al. (2022) investigated scheduling algorithms that incor­
porate battery constraints, optimizing AGV routes to include 
necessary detours to charging stations while minimizing 
downtime. These approaches often employ mixed-integer 
linear programming (MILP) models, which allow for the 
simultaneous optimization of multiple parameters, includ­
ing energy consumption and task scheduling. Similarly, 
Dang et  al. (2021) presented a comprehensive study on 
scheduling heterogeneous AGVs with battery limitations, 
demonstrating the effectiveness of their model in reducing 
energy consumption while maintaining system efficiency.
Genetic algorithms (GAs) have been widely applied in 
AGV scheduling due to their flexibility and ability to find 
near-optimal solutions in complex environments. Chaudhry 
et  al. (2022) investigated the integrated scheduling of 
machines and AGVs in a flexible job shop environment 
using genetic algorithms. Their study emphasized the poten­
tial of GAs to handle dynamic scheduling environments, 
where the number of tasks and vehicles can vary signifi­
cantly. Recent studies continue to build on these founda­
tions, exploring hybrid approaches and improved genetic 
algorithms to enhance scheduling efficiency in flexible 
manufacturing systems (Meng et al. 2023). Sun et al. (2022)

In designing the architecture, several critical challenges 
should be addressed to meet the objectives effectively. 
These challenges arise from the limitations inherent in 
Cloud-to-Edge technologies, particularly in the context of 
AGV scheduling in sophisticated manufacturing environ­
ments. A significant challenge is the limited processing 
power of edge devices compared to cloud servers, restrict­
ing the volume of data that can be processed locally at the 
edge. This often necessitates offloading data to the cloud for 
more in-depth analysis. Furthermore, edge devices are con­
strained by limited storage capacity, complicating the local 
storage and analysis of large datasets, again requiring cloud 
assistance.
Another crucial challenge lies in connectivity. Edge 
devices frequently operate in environments with limited 
or intermittent connectivity, complicating the transmission 
of data to the cloud for processing and real-time decision-
making. These connectivity issues directly affect the feasi­
bility of real-time analytics at the edge, which is essential 
for dynamic AGV scheduling. Security concerns also come 
into play, as edge devices are more vulnerable to threats like 
hacking and data breaches, potentially compromising the 
entire system’s security. Ensuring robust security protocols 
for both edge devices and data is fundamental to safeguard­
ing system integrity.
Moreover, integrating a diverse array of edge devices 
and cloud platforms introduces complex interoperability 
challenges, necessitating significant time and resources to 
ensure seamless communication across systems. Cost con­
siderations are also critical, as the deployment and manage­
ment of a comprehensive edge computing infrastructure can 
lead to substantial capital and operational expenses.

learn long-term dependencies.

Our mathematical model is a variant of the one proposed

6  Conclusions and future works
This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for 
optimizing the scheduling of Automated Guided Vehicles 
(AGVs) in intelligent manufacturing environments. The 
framework focuses on enhancing operational efficiency, 
energy management, and battery life. The proposed frame­
work integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, 
machine learning, and a hybrid cloud-to-edge architecture, 
offering a robust solution for the challenges faced in modern 
production settings.
The framework was designed to support dynamic sched­
uling through a multi-layered approach that combines 
cloud-based analytics with edge computing for real-time 
decision-making. The cloud-to-edge architecture distrib­
utes computational tasks effectively: the cloud layer handles 
large-scale data analysis, machine learning model training, 
and historical data processing, while the edge layer focuses 
on the immediate execution of scheduling decisions. This 
design ensures flexibility and adaptability in responding 
to the rapidly changing conditions typical of manufactur­
ing environments. The integration of a digital twin within 
the framework allowed for the virtual representation of 
the manufacturing facility, enabling precise simulations of 
AGV operations based on real-world layouts provided by a 
partner of the Zero-SWARM project.
The proposed scheduling solution leverages a novel 
machine learning-based approach to optimize task alloca­
tion. At the core of this solution is a machine learning model 
for predicting the state of charge (SoC) of AGV batteries, 
which forms the basis for calculating the lambda parameter. 
The battery SoC predictor uses historical and real-time data 
to accurately forecast battery levels over a user-defined time 
horizon, considering factors such as energy consumption 
patterns and operational conditions. This predictive capa­
bility allows the scheduling model to adapt dynamically, 
assigning tasks based on the real-time status and expected 
battery performance of each AGV.
The scheduler then uses the calculated lambda param­
eter to optimize task assignments. This parameter reflects 
the degradation state of the battery and allows for a more 
nuanced scheduling process that accounts for energy effi­
ciency by dynamically adjusting the weight of battery-
related constraints. The lambda parameter serves as a

to significant time and cost implications due to unplanned 
downtime.
Future work will also include a detailed cost-benefit anal­
ysis to quantitatively assess the economic impact of the pro­
posed scheduling framework. This will involve evaluating 
both the initial deployment costs and the long-term opera­
tional savings, particularly in terms of reduced energy con­
sumption, maintenance requirements, and downtime. Such 
analysis will be developed in collaboration with the indus­
trial partners of the Zero-SWARM project to strengthen the 
practical relevance of the ongoing field trials.
Finally, the real-world validation of the framework in 
an industrial setting remains a critical step towards gen­
eralizing the findings, going out the setups driven by the 
Zero-SWARM project. Addressing practical implementa­
tion challenges, such as data security, system interoperabil­
ity, and latency in edge-to-cloud communications, will be 
essential to refining the proposed approach for deployment 
in actual smart manufacturing environments.

Abstract: Optimizing the scheduling of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) is a critical task in the context of smart manufacturing, particularly in Industry 4.0, where operational efficiency, sustainability, and adaptability are key drivers of innovation. This paper introduces an innovative scheduling model incorporating real-time AGV battery status as a key parameter, using a machine learning algorithm to predict energy consumption and optimize task allocation accordingly. The primary objective is to extend AGV battery life, reduce energy consumption, and contribute to environmental sustainability, all while maintaining high operational efficiency. In addition to the scheduling algorithm, we present a comprehensive appli­ cation framework designed to integrate this optimization model into real-world factory environments. This architecture leverages cloud-edge computing to process real-time data from AGVs, enabling dynamic scheduling adjustments and seamless execution of tasks. The proposed approach has been experimentally validated, demonstrating improvements in energy efficiency when compared to a conventional AGV scheduling strategy. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of our solution in improving energy efficiency while maintaining high performance in AGV operations. By providing the necessary infrastructure for data input, processing, and output implementation, the framework ensures that the algorithm can be effectively deployed and scaled in industrial settings. This research offers a robust solution for AGV scheduling, balancing operational efficiency with sustainability.
